Lessons.Title: The Root of the Problem
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Recover a positive linear scale from a prescribed volume factor with the cube-root function; contrast it with the square root needed for surface area.
Mathematical model: If volume ratio q=k³ with k>0, length factor is k=∛q Use the real positive cube root A known volume ratio q implies area ratio q^(2/3)
Application and limitations: Nonnegative geometric volumes yield nonnegative scale factors Positive nondegenerate solids require q>0

Teacher rubric (0–8): four 0/1/2 teacher criteria cover exact root modelling, eight-point source cube-root plot and shrinking average change, source satellite sqrt-vs-cubert target factors and invalid k4 critique, and eight source Practice with correct domain and units.
Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 7, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

Source 7.1 The Number That Cubes (5 min): unit cube side1, new volumes27,1000,1001,7 demand positive k=cuberoot(V); answers 3,10,about10.0033,about1.9129. Explain 27→3 is a cube root not division by3, and use original simple cube drawings rather than any publisher images. Nonnegative input0 gives k0 collapsed limit; actual geometric nondegenerate cube requires V>0.

Source 7.2 Thinking Inside the Box (20 min): source shipper's basic box is cube side1 foot, volume1ft³; source new 8ft³→k2,10ft³→k≈2.1544. Complete exact ORIGINAL table of x volumes0,1,5,8,10,15,20,27 and y=cuberoot(x) rounded hundredths0,1,1.71,2,2.15,2.47,2.71,3. Plot graph x in CUBIC FEET and y DIMENSIONLESS scale, smooth increasing concave down for x>0. Compare additional4ft³ from21 to25 changes k by cubert25−cubert21≈.15, whereas from1 to5 increases k cubert5−1≈.71; equal added volume does not mean equal added length factor.

Source 7.2 double-volume 10 to20 changes scale by multiplicative factor cubert2≈1.25992, not doubling; it grows from about2.1544 to2.7144. Source graph and earlier y=sqrt(x) both start at(0,0), increase and flatten with x>0; no copyrighted applet reproduction or app UI verification. Student must explain how cube-root function inverts volume k³, and why k becomes small changes for larger volumes.

Source 7.3 Satellite Scale Factors (10 min): original hypothetical satellite solar-panel surface area5.4ft², interior volume1.2ft³. Target area21.6ft² requires k=sqrt(21.6/5.4)=sqrt4=2. Target volume4.05ft³ requires k=cubert(4.05/1.2)=cubert3.375=1.5. Source fake student suggestion k4 for area erroneously uses area ratio rather than sqrt; peers explicitly critique. The two design goals require DIFFERENT uniform size factors and therefore cannot both be satisfied exactly with one chosen k unless constraints change.

Source 7.3 optional extension: if the NUMERICAL VALUE of satellite surface area in square feet equals numerical volume in cubic feet, solve 5.4k²=1.2k³ for k>0 -> k=4.5. This is merely numerical equality of quantities with different dimensions and units and NOT a literal equality of physical area and volume. Under k=4.5 their numerical values both109.35, but units ft² versus ft³ differ. Clarify model semantics and optionally compare physical constraints instead of recommending real satellite sizing.

Source student summary source prism initial volume5 to320 yields k=cubert(320/5)=4, graph k=cubert(V/5) with points (0,0),(5,1),(40,2),(135,3),(320,4). Cylinder initial surface area35 to218.75 gives k=sqrt(218.75/35)=sqrt6.25=2.5. Preserve earlier first-party correct example 16→54 cubic units factor1.5, volume64× leads to surface16×, cube343 side7; those are not the original source figures.

Source Practice P1-P8: P1 original volume8 desired216→k3,1→k1/2,1000→k5. P2 k=cubert(V/7) true points A(0,0), D(7,1), G(56,2); B(1,1), C(1,7), E(14,2), F(49,2), H(27,3) wrong. P6 y=sqrt(x/9) true choices A(0,0), E(9,1), H(36,2) only. P7 flyer area576in² scale1/4 ->36in². P8 right triangle S90,T45,ST3ft implies other leg SU3ft. Lessons.Title: Speaking of Scaling
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Coordinate length, surface-area and volume scale factors in both forward and reverse directions from any one known ratio, and communicate missing information.
Mathematical model: For uniform dilation, ratios are k,k²,k³ Use positive roots for inverse problems Reversed area and volume factors are 1/k² and 1/k³
Application and limitations: The type of given ratio must be specified to find the others Ask whether a value is a length, area or volume ratio

Teacher rubric (0–8): four teacher-scored 0/1/2 criteria evaluate source cone positive square-root inverse4.5, two independent first-party information-gap rounds with correct information protocol and dimension classification, original Jumbo Can maximum k2 and cost2.32 with model assumptions, and seven source Practice exact values with units and teacher explanation.
Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 8, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

Source 8.1 Going Backwards (5 min): original cone has base area36pi cm² and dilated base729pi cm². The base AREA multiplier729/36=20.25, while corresponding LENGTH dilation k=sqrt20.25=4.5, not20.25. Compare 4²=16, 5²=25 and justify positive k; its volume factor k³=91.125 if all dimensions scale uniformly. Students critique their initial answer and communicate one, two, three-dimensional ratio roles.

Source 8.2 Info Gap Originals and Dilations (20 min): source uses TWO rounds of privately held problem/data cards. Partner holding data asks precisely WHAT given and WHY needed, reveals ONLY an asked-for original datum, never computes partner's unknowns; problem holder requests whether known measurement is length, surface area or volume, then recovers missing ratios from k,k²,k³ and independently solves. Swap cards and roles for round two and compare two valid methods for dilated cylinder volume: direct V=pi r²h with scaled radius/height versus original volume multiplied by k³. Publisher blackline data contents not publicly accessible as independent materials; substitute original Edulytiks cards rather than assert exact original numbers.

Source 8.3 Jumbo Can (15 min OPTIONAL): first reading identifies basic cans, second quantifies material cost $.04 per original can and juice fill $.27 per original can, third explains maximum material budget $.16 for scaled can with similar shape. MATERIAL cost scales with exterior surface area ∝k², so $.04k²≤$.16 gives largest positive k=2, doubling both height AND radius. JUICE volume cost scales k³, so $.27*8=$2.16, material $.16, combined per jumbo can $2.32 under strictly linear per-area/material and volume/juice price assumptions. Ask for two labelled first-party cylinder diagrams and caveats: seam, wall thickness, lids, label, waste and setup affect actual cost. No real production quote or product safety is certified.

Source 8.3 optional Burj Khalifa to Eiffel scale: source as of2019 historical heights and outside research required; without independently supplied actual building height and units cannot assign one unique numeric model ratio from a30-inch tower model. Students state k=30in/actual Burj height in inches and Eiffel model length=k*(Eiffel actual length in inches), only compute numeric if legitimate sources/units available. Do not import unverified historical record or internet measurement into protected source parity claims.

Source student summary original aquarium10in high,10in wide,14in long with nominal capacity5 gallons and surface area760in². A model museum aquarium135 gallons has volume factor135/5=27, positive k=cubert27=3 and dimensions30 by30 by42 inches, source exterior surface760*9=6840in². Note nominal5gallons is not literally the 1400 cubic inches geometric exterior volume without accounting for wall thickness and capacity; physical real aquarium volume and numerical design model are approximate. Source teacher conclusion wrongly phrases dividing new volume by old when given surface areas: correct area ratio is new surface/old surface, then sqrt, then cube to get volume ratio.

Source Practice P1-P7: P1 individual muffin serving1 scaled to serve100 by volume assumption requires length k=cubert100≈4.6416, decorative-paper use grows k²=100^(2/3)≈21.54 times for geometrically similar liner surface coverage. P2 game box original height8cm, wrap surface1408cm² vs travel198cm², area ratio198/1408=9/64, k=3/8, new height3cm. P3 cone SA360pi in² and V800pi in³, image SA2250pi => SA factor25/4=6.25, k=5/2, volume800pi*(125/8)=12500pi in³. P4 tanker model1gal to8000gal length factor cbrt8000=20. P5 k=cubert(V/4) two examples V4 k1 and V32 k2. P6 cube side3in original SA6*9=54in² and V27in³; k1/2 gives new side1.5in, SA13.5in² and V27/8=3.375in³. P7 circle area100pi→25pi gives k=sqrt1/4=1/2 choice C. Original teacher-locked 8.4 Dog Food Bags unavailable; use first-party paired card + can cost teacher paper review.

Lessons.Title: Cylinder Volumes
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Derive and use V=πr²h for right or oblique circular cylinders, and compute volumes of composite figures and rotational solids without confusing radius with diameter.
Mathematical model: A cylinder has constant cross-sectional disk area B=πr² Volume=Bh=πr²h with perpendicular height h Cavalieri gives same volume for equal base area and perpendicular height
Application and limitations: Volumes add for disjoint interiors and subtract removed pieces Use consistent cubic units

Teacher rubric (0–8): four 0/1/2 human criteria score prism/cylinder same-B layer proof; original water transfer preserving36*pi base area; original axis-labelled rotational A=87*pi B=96*pi and alternative 99*pi with solid/hollow reasoning; source Practice seven problems exact/equivalent values, dimensional reasoning and protected-image cautions. No online grades are claimed.
Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 9, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

Source 9.1 The Same But Different (5 minutes): original teacher displays two solids, asks what measurements are required for each and how prism and cylinder methods are same/different. Prism B is length times width or a given polygon base area; cylinder B=pi*r^2 using a RADIUS (not diameter), with the perpendicular height h. Both V=B*h for constant-area congruent horizontal layers. Teacher reviews original figure rather than inventing missing dimensions or names; students compare strategies with a partner before synthesis.

Source 9.2 Water Transfer (15 minutes): original RECTANGULAR PRISM base dimensions 9cm by 4*pi cm, so area9*(4*pi)=36*pi cm^2. Original CYLINDER base radius6cm, so area pi*(6)^2=36*pi cm^2. At water height1cm in prism, water volume36*pi cm^3; transferred into empty cylinder of equal base area yields height1cm. At prism water height3cm, volume108*pi cm^3 and cylinder water height3cm. Require student physical sketches of unit-height layers, explicit comparable volumes and V/B reasoning; when actual container capacity/height constraints are not stated, treat filling as idealized nonoverflow volume preservation.

Source 9.3 Revisiting Rotation (15 minutes), source shaded grid A: vertical rotation axis x=3, lower rectangle x from3 to8 for y1..4, upper rectangle x3..5 for y4..7 (one grid unit=1cm). Disjoint interior layers give lower right cylinder radius5 height3 volume75*pi cm^3, upper cylinder radius2 height3 volume12*pi cm^3, TOTAL87*pi cm^3. Do not conflate lower radius5 with diameter5. Independent check by slicing along y through each constant cross-section.

Source 9.3 source shaded grid B: vertical axis x=3, region rectangle x6..8 and y1..7. Rotating creates HOLLOW right cylinder outer radius8-3=5cm, inner radius6-3=3cm, height6cm, so V=pi*(5^2-3^2)*6=96*pi cm^3. This is outer-minus-inner ring area, not solid radius2 cylinder and not a torus. Original optional horizontal rotation of figure A about bottom y=1 instead yields exactly99*pi cm^3: x3..5 a filled disk of radius6 for axial width2 gives72*pi, and x5..8 a filled disk of radius3 for axial width3 gives27*pi, yielding exactly99*pi. Distinguish the alternative axis from original vertical 87*pi.

Source 9.3 optional comparison: cylinder radius r height h: height tripled→3*pi*r^2*h (factor3), radius tripled→9*pi*r^2*h (factor9), cube edge s tripled→(3s)^3=27*s^3 (factor27). Do not mistake radius tripling for a length-only volume factor3 because base area scales quadratically. Source synthesis contrasts butter, nuts, pencils approximable by constant-layer cylinder/prism composites with pyramid/cone/sphere whose base-parallel cross-sectional areas change with height; V=B*h with one fixed B is not valid for such varying sections.

Source student summary 9.4 hollow cylinder: horizontal axis y=1, filled source rectangle x4..9 and y2..5, outer radius4, inner radius1, cylinder axial length5, volume5*pi*(4^2-1^2)=75*pi cubic units. Demonstrate outer80*pi minus inner5*pi. Original teacher-login Cylinder Strategies cool-down remains restricted; Edulytiks first-party paper investigation and teacher scoring replace it without claiming identity.

Source Practice P1-P7: P1 horizontal axis y=1, shaded rectangle x3..9,y1..4 gives SOLID cylinder radius3cm axial length6cm and volume pi*3^2*6=54*pi cm^3. P2 four original region/axis pairs have distinct constructions; source corresponding output IMAGE numbers are inaccessible, so avoid guessed matching. A: x3..9,y2..4 around y1 annular radii1/3 h6 gives48*pi; B: x4..10,y2..4 around x2 annular radii2/8 h2 gives120*pi; C: x4..8,y2..4 around x2 annular radii2/6 h2 gives64*pi; D: x4..8,y3..5 around y1 annular radii2/4 h4 gives48*pi; teacher matches actual visual identities. P3: cylinder r4in h3in→48*pi in^3; cylinder r3in h4in→36*pi in^3; hexagonal prism B30.5cm^2 h6.5cm→198.25cm^3; triangular prism base right legs6/7ft area21ft^2 h5ft→105ft^3. P4 bagel volume25 times: linear scale cbrt25≈2.9, same-thickness cream-cheese coating scales with area by (cbrt25)^2≈8.5 times to tenth (idealized coverage). P5 toothpaste original plastic1224cm^2 travel306cm^2 implies area factor1/4, length scale1/2, original box8cm becomes4cm choice C. P6 volume32→4 ratio1/8 k=cbrt(1/8)=1/2 choice D. P7 cube side4in surface area96in^2 volume64in^3, k.25→edge1in surface6in^2 volume1in^3. Include exact-oracle, equivalent, incorrect, boundary, malformed responses in authoring.

Lessons.Title: Cross Sections and Volume
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Apply Cavalieri's principle correctly: solids of equal height with equal cross-sectional areas at each corresponding level have equal volumes; compare oblique prisms and cylinders.
Mathematical model: Equal-height solids with matching areas of parallel sections at every corresponding height have equal volumes Require all levels, not one Constant A gives V=Ah
Application and limitations: Equal base area or one equal slice alone does not force equal volume Check all corresponding levels

Teacher rubric (0–8): four human 0/1/2 criteria score source coin/index-card shift explanation, all-height Cavalieri conditions and non-converse counterexample, three source pairs with exact volumes and perpendicular height distinction, and original eight Practice solutions with vase/figure limits and consistent cubic units.

Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 10, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

Source 10.1 Two Stacks of Coins (5 min): original equal COUNT of identical coins stacked straight up A (right cylinder model) and shifted sideways B (oblique cylinder model). Each coin is a thin cylindrical SLAB with equal volume; lateral shift preserves base disk area and total perpendicular vertical height, so the total volume is unchanged even though lateral edges are slanted. Students describe perpendicular height rather than mistakenly substituting slant edge length, and explain why discrete coin stacks only approximate smooth cylinders.

Source 10.2 Rectangular Prism, Shifted (15 min): draw an original tall stack of equal rectangular index cards of area B, constant physical thickness and total perpendicular height h, then shift each card laterally without deformation. Each horizontal plane through interior of either right or oblique prism has equal-area rectangle cross section B and corresponding heights are unchanged. Therefore both volumes equal B*h. Three original student prompts require paired sketches of right and skewed sections, prediction as plane moves up/down, and an all-heights proof. Physically shifting cards does NOT convert the horizontal cross-sectional rectangle into a parallelogram: that could be the side face under a vertical cutting plane instead. GeoGebra source applet not claimed connected.

Source 10.2 Cavalieri Principle teacher theorem: IF solids have the SAME perpendicular HEIGHT and, for EACH matching height t, the cross sections by planes parallel to the same base plane have EQUAL AREA, THEN they have EQUAL VOLUME. Shape of cross section may differ (circular disk vs rectangle), as may obliqueness; equal volume cannot be deduced from ONE equal slice or equal base areas only if slice functions differ. Proof based on accumulating arbitrarily thin equal-area slabs; source states full formal proof lies beyond this course. As a counterexample, a cylinder B20,h6 has volume120 while a cone same base area and height has volume40 because intermediate sections differ.

Source 10.3 Equal Volumes? (15 min): three original pairs. Pair1 oblique cylinder r3 PERPENDICULAR height7 and slanted lateral edge10, compared with right cylinder r3 height10: volumes63*pi and90*pi, NOT equal; slant10 cannot substitute for height7. Pair2 right cone r3 h5 and oblique cone with same circular base r3 and perpendicular h5: each parallel cross section at apex-based fractional height t has disk area9*pi*t², hence equal volumes by Cavalieri despite offset apex; from already-known cone formula both15*pi. Pair3 triangular prism right triangle base legs3 and4, perpendicular height5 versus rectangular prism base1 by6 and perpendicular height5: both base area6 and volume30, equal even though planar shapes differ. Students must justify yes/no for all three and independently revise after comparing peers.

Source 10.3 class synthesis: a tilted cylinder whose perpendicular height is25 and radius10 has volume pi*10²*25=2500*pi cubic units, while marked diagonal edge30 is irrelevant. Source student summary compares oblique circular cylinder with right rectangular prism each horizontal slice area6cm² and equal height, so volumes agree; pairs of square-base right and oblique pyramids with source base side5 h7 also have matching levels and equal volume (source does not require students to derive pyramid formula yet). A prism/cylinder with constant section area B at all heights has V=B*h for oblique OR right versions, but not a general cone/pyramid/sphere because areas vary with t.

Source Practice P1-P8: P1 vase with base area B and height h but unspecified cross-sectional profiles in accessible original text: V relative to B*h cannot be inferred from B and h alone, and original image must be viewed to select A/B/C/D; if all intermediate sections constant B then equality, but vase might taper or bulge. P2 cylinder radius3.5cm h12.5cm volume pi*3.5²*12.5=153.125*pi≈481.056cm³; right rectangular prism6.4cm by4cm by12.5cm volume320cm³; cylinder contains more. P3 zigzag rectangular-slice crystal vase outer area6*3=18 in², h10in, zero-thickness capacity180in³; with walls .5in EACH side and bottom .5in, interior horizontal dims5 by2 in and height9.5in, approximate usable interior volume95in³, assuming consistent horizontal interior rectangle and ignoring join/neck irregularities. P4 right prism and cylinder have constant B sections, cone and sphere do not. P5 original prior U05L09 figure rotation image not provided in text: require marked diagram and axis before numeric volume. P6 volume2 to128 factor64 -> k4, SA10*4²=160 square units. P7 SA50 to200 implies k2 choice B. P8 e.g. cylinder/prism have all congruent nonempty sections parallel to bases. Original teacher-login 10.4 Drawing Solids Cool-down locked; independent Edulytiks paper slice comparison scored by teacher.

Teacher rubric (0–8): four human 0/1/2 criteria assess source A/B right-triangle heights without invented labels, choice A-G three-solids student justification and correctness, source Cayan Tower 1995-area/17-core/306-height gross volume with source 57-vs-58 caveat, and nine indexed practice answers and figure/angle ambiguities.

Source orientation: Illustrative Mathematics Geometry First Edition (2019–2021), Unit 5 Lesson 11, CC BY 4.0. Independent first-party Edulytiks examples; no publisher artwork or protected assessments.

Source 11.1 New Heights (10 min): original source presents two figure-only heights A and B; first can be found by adding a perpendicular height and applying Pythagoras to a right-triangle relation, with source teacher noting one result rounds16.0; second oblique cylinder features a source40-degree angle requiring an appropriate sine projection and DEGREE-mode calculator rather than using Pythagoras without a full right triangle's two lengths. The original figure's marked lengths and edge-angle orientation are not available in student text, so teacher must inspect diagram before grading exact A/B heights. Perpendicular height is distinct from a lateral edge or sloped diameter.

Source 11.2 The Choice is Yours (15 min): students inspect actual SEVEN source solids A through G, choose two easiest and two hardest BEFORE calculating, justify choices in peer discussion, then select THREE solids including at least one from each difficulty list. Original picture-only A-G dimensions are absent from source HTML text, so do not invent a matching output or replace the student's choice with unrelated items; teacher supplies original images. Students solve selected cases using Bh, Pythagoras, right-triangle trigonometry, decomposition of nonoverlapping prism/cylinder volumes, units and reasonable tenths.

Source 11.2 optional rotation extension: original eight-sided 2D diagram spun about vertical C line with dimensions A,B,C,D and total desired volume297*pi; it requires labelled source figure to establish what each of A,B,C,D measures, so an ungrounded positive integer solution would be false source parity. A first-party independent bounded alternative is an annular cylinder of outer radius5, inner radius2 and height11, giving (25-4)*11*pi=231*pi; require exact source marked diagram before asserting original297*pi configuration.

Source 11.3 The Cayan Tower (10 min): original 2019 historical tower classroom model has approximate height306m, identically shaped floors rotating about the core. Teacher-facing text says chevron B=57*35=1995m², while accessible image description says top-to-bottom chevron span58m; this is a REAL SOURCE-METADATA CONTRADICTION. Use 1995m² for arithmetic expressly sourced to textual stated area, and require original floor-plan image verification before claiming 57 versus58 geometric dimension. A matched CHEVRON base-parallel slice at every height has area1995m² regardless of floor orientation, so idealized gross tower volume1995*306=610470m³; model core circle diameter17m radius8.5m has cross-sectional area72.25*pi m², core volume72.25*pi*306=22108.5*pi m³. Gross core fraction (72.25*pi/1995)*100 ≈11.38%, assuming uniform core across306m and treating gross outer area including core. Do not confuse actual net usable floor volume with gross model or present historical building dimensions as recent survey.

Source 11.3 teacher discussion: shifting/rotating congruent horizontal floors changes side faces but not base-parallel area at each height; Cavalieri compares gross rotated tower with hypothetical straight aligned tower. Physical floor thickness is positive and a mathematical plane cross section is 2D without thickness. Compute idealized core fraction as ratio of areas because heights cancel, and distinguish exact symbolic result from approximate real building estimates. Source student summary separate independent cylinder r5cm, diagonal15cm across diameter10cm: perpendicular height sqrt(15²-10²)=sqrt125=5sqrt5 cm, cylinder volume25*pi*sqrt125≈878.1cm³; preserve earlier correct independent worked examples rather than overwriting them.

Source Practice P1-P9: P1 source right triangular base AC4, AB5 hypotenuse, right at C gives BC3; with prism height CF8, V=(4*3/2)*8=48 cubic units, conditional on diagram confirmation of CF as perpendicular prism length. P2 oblique cylinder base r2, lateral translation6sqrt2 at45degrees to base plane gives perpendicular h=6sqrt2*sin45=6, V=pi*2²*6=24*pi cubic units. P3 prism V80in³ h5in needs base area16in², options A square4x4, B rectangle2x8, E heart area16; options C disk r2 area4pi and D right triangle legs4 area8 wrong. P4 water bottle with base B and height h cannot decide exact comparison to Bh without actual curved source silhouette and sections; teacher reviews source picture. P5 any solid with ALL horizontal parallel-base sections squares side3, perpendicular h10 has V=9*10=90 cubic units choice C even if walls curved. P6 rotation about source horizontal axis picture missing, no invented radius. P7 original volume6 area22 scaled new area198, area multiplier9 k3 and volume6*27=162 cubic units. P8 Khufu original square base231, height144, cross section side154 gives k=154/231=2/3, plane height above base144*(1-2/3)=48m (distance below apex96m); distinguish two height origins. P9 the angle bisector of ANY angle halves the angle by definition, choice B certainly true. Statements A/D about 'the' isosceles angle bisector or median only hold if it is FROM THE APEX to the base, not arbitrary vertex median/bisector, so require original diagram and intended referent before authoring unconditional A/D. WorkedExamples.Title: Oblique prism: missing perpendicular height
WorkedExamples.Question: An oblique prism has base area 14 cm² and lateral edge length 10 cm making angle 30° with the base plane. Find its volume.
WorkedExamples.Method: Resolve the lateral edge into its normal height component.
Steps: The perpendicular height is h=10sin30° because the edge makes a 30° angle with its projection on the base plane.
Since sin30°=1/2, h=5 cm; the slanted 10 cm is NOT the volume height.
WorkedExamples.Check: Height is measured perpendicular to base; use degree mode.

Lessons.Title: Prisms and Pyramids
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: Contrast prisms, pyramids, cylinders and cones by their changing versus constant parallel cross sections and predict the one-third volume relationship.
Mathematical model: Prism parallel slices are congruent; pyramid slices shrink toward one apex Identify base, apex and perpendicular height Equal base and height do not imply equal volume
Application and limitations: A pyramid and prism with same base area B and height h have ratio 1:3 Use established decomposition/Cavalieri formula

Authentic source-specific activity: Draw labelled constant-section and taper-section sequences and justify why cone/pyramid differ from prism/cylinder. Teacher reviews arguments. Teacher rubric (0–4): correct diagram/units, explicit premises, reliable calculations, and an independently justified interpretation. Original drawings and written reasoning require teacher scoring.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cone vs cylinder
KeyConcepts.Definition: Cone parallel disks taper; cylinder disks have constant area
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equal base and height do not imply equal volume
KeyConcepts.Example: Cone volume is one third matching cylinder
